keeping.days: Every song is deleted 30 days after it’s made, along with everything saved with it. Until then, anyone with its link can open it.
keeping.intro: What I keep depends on the kind of file you upload.
keeping.kept_file: It’s saved with the song, because the song plays from it.
keeping.kept_sheet: It’s held in memory while homr and Gemini read it, and then it’s dropped. Only what they read is saved: the notes, the chords, the title and the tempo.

picture.balls: Each staff gets a ball for each note of its biggest chord. A ball lands on every notehead as it sounds and arcs to the next one, higher when the notes are further apart. It leaves a glowing trail with a soft reflection on the floor.
picture.camera: The camera changes shots through the song: from above the staves, a sweep from the front, low along the floor, or down the staff lines. It changes at each section of the arrangement, or every eight bars if there isn’t one.
picture.clock: Every ball’s position comes from the music’s clock, so a ball reaches a note at the moment you hear it. When you pause, the balls slow down over about a third of a second and stop along their paths.
picture.engrave: The score is laid out by OpenSheetMusicDisplay, a library that draws sheet music in the browser. It draws the whole song as one long line of staves, and it draws it as an SVG, which describes every staff line, note and symbol as a shape instead of as pixels.
picture.floor: The scene is 3D, built with three.js. Instead of turning the SVG into a flat picture and laying it on the floor, every shape in it becomes 3D geometry. That keeps the notes sharp when the camera moves in close or looks along the floor, where a picture would start to blur.
picture.from_midi: The page writes a score from the file’s notes.
picture.from_musicxml: The page draws the file’s own score.
picture.from_sheet: The page uses the score homr wrote while reading it, with an extra staff for the chords Gemini found.
picture.line: One challenge with SVG was keeping a long song on a single line. OpenSheetMusicDisplay starts a new line once a sheet is 32,767 pixels wide. That number is the widest a canvas can be in most browsers. The library can draw on a canvas as well as in SVG, and it applies the same limit to both, even though SVG doesn’t need it. A seven-minute song wrapped onto three lines, and the balls lost the music after the first one. The score here is only drawn as SVG, so I lifted the limit.
picture.loop: When the song ends, the balls rise toward the next copy of the score, so playing it again carries straight on.
picture.source: The floor never shows the image or PDF you uploaded. The score on it is drawn by the page, from a source that depends on the kind of file.
picture.title: The scene

reading.background: Reading a sheet takes a while, so it carries on in the background. You can leave the page, and a notification appears when the song is ready.
reading.bars: One detail that matters here is keeping the chords aligned with the music. I give Gemini the number of bars homr found on each line, so it has some structure to work with rather than trying to interpret the entire page independently.
reading.chords: The chords play softly under the notes, as a bass note and up to four chord tones held until the next chord. If homr can’t read a sheet, only the chords play.
reading.done: Once the reading is complete, the API saves the result and the browser can turn it into a performance.
reading.how_files: They’re relatively straightforward. The browser reads the file directly, so every note is available exactly as written. It then sends the file to the API, which saves it as a song.
reading.how_sheet: It’s a different story. A photograph or PDF doesn’t tell you where the notes are in a format a computer can play. Kinetic Light first needs to understand what’s written on the page.
reading.intro: There are two ways to get music into Kinetic Light, and they need quite different approaches.
reading.readers: First, [homr](https://github.com/liebharc/homr), an optical music recognition system running on its own server, reads the notes. Then Gemini fills in the information homr doesn’t reliably capture: chord symbols, the title and tempo.
reading.repair: homr sometimes reads a note one value too long, which pushes the notes after it out of the bar. When a bar’s longest note is exactly twice what fits, it’s halved before the score is drawn. Aerith’s Theme had a dotted whole note in bar 16 where the sheet has a dotted half.
reading.steps: I split that process into two steps.
reading.title: Teaching it to read music

sound.answers: The drum sound decides what plays at each step. On the drum kit, the lo-fi kit and the LinnDrum, a hi-hat plays on every step, a kick on each bar’s first beat and under long bass notes, and a snare on every second beat. The drum machine plays a kick on every beat, a clap on every second beat and an open hi-hat between the beats. Hand percussion plays the drum kit’s pattern on congas and a shaker, with a high bongo between the beats.
sound.arrange: Before a song is ready, a text model arranges it. It gets an outline of the song instead of the notes: the title, the tempo, the beats in a bar and where notes start in each bar. From that it picks the piano, the drums, the zoom, the color and the glow. It also writes the drums in sections, each with a one-bar pattern and a fill on its last bar.
sound.beat: What the drums play depends on the song.
sound.drum_kit: It’s a recorded acoustic drum kit.
sound.drum_linndrum: It’s the LinnDrum, a drum machine that plays recordings of real drums.
sound.drum_lofi: It’s the same drum kit, recorded lo-fi.
sound.drum_machine: It’s the Roland TR-808, a drum machine that makes its sounds electronically.
sound.drum_none: Only the sound you picked plays, with no drums.
sound.drum_percussion: It’s recorded congas, bongos and a shaker.
sound.drums: There are six choices for the drums.
sound.drums_arranged: The drums play the sections the text model wrote when it arranged the song.
sound.drums_midi: Its own drum part plays, even after the song is arranged, with each General MIDI drum on the closest sample.
sound.drums_other: The page writes a beat from the song’s own rhythm. The diagram below shows how.
sound.once: A song is arranged once and keeps its arrangement, so everyone who opens its link hears the same thing. Changing a setting afterwards only changes the page you have open.
sound.title: The sound and the beat
sound.voice_grand: It’s a recorded grand piano with no effects.
sound.voice_sixteen: It’s the grand piano playing every note twice, once as written and once an octave lower, with a brighter tone, an echo and some reverb. The name comes from the organ stop that sounds an octave below the written note.
sound.voice_synth: It’s a synthesizer that Tone.js generates instead of a recording, with an echo and some reverb.
sound.voice_upright: It’s a recorded upright piano with a little reverb.
sound.voice_wurlitzer: It’s a recorded Wurlitzer electric piano with a little reverb. $t(credit_wurlitzer).
sound.voices: Tone.js, a library for making music in the browser, plays the notes. You can pick one of five sounds.

tracking.allowance: Reading a sheet costs money, so each visitor can read a few sheets a day, shown on the badge under the description. The count covers the last 24 hours, not the calendar day. When none are left, the form is hidden and only the badge shows.
tracking.session: You don’t need an account. On your first visit, the site checks that you’re human with Cloudflare Turnstile and gives your browser a token. The songs you make are tied to that token, which is how the Songs list knows which ones are yours.
tracking.title: How I know which songs are yours

what_this_is.idea: I came across something online that got me thinking: what if I could build something that reads sheet music and turns it into a live performance?
what_this_is.piano: I’ve always wanted to play the piano. I also have a soft spot for piano-infused melodic techno, where a piano melody sits somewhere between an instrument and an electronic soundscape.
what_this_is.presence: Not just playing the notes, but giving them a visual presence.
what_this_is.summary: You can give it a MIDI or MusicXML file, or upload a photo or PDF of sheet music. It reads the music, plays it on a piano with a drum beat, and projects the score onto a dark floor. As the music plays, balls of light move from note to note, following the melody and chords.
what_this_is.three: The idea was to bring together three things: reading music, making music, and visualising it.

credit_wurlitzer: Wurlitzer samples by Greg Sullivan, [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/)

beat.description: The page reads three things from the song’s notes: the grid the notes fall on, which is eighths, triplets or sixteenths, whichever nine in ten notes fit; where long bass notes start; and how loud the notes are on average. It then goes through the song one step of the grid at a time. At each step it asks whether the step is on a beat or between beats, which beat of the bar it is, whether a long bass note starts there, and whether it’s the first step of a round. The drum sound picked in the player decides which drum plays for each answer. The result is a drum part at the notes’ loudness, played with the song.
beat.title: How the page writes a beat

picture.description: The score, which depends on the kind of file, is drawn by OpenSheetMusicDisplay as one long line of staves in SVG. Every shape in the SVG becomes 3D geometry on the floor of the three.js scene, and the positions of the noteheads, staves and bars feed the ball paths. The clock, which is where the song is at the moment you hear it, drives the ball paths and the camera, so the balls and the shots follow the music.
picture.title: From the score to the scene

reading.description: The browser reads a MIDI or MusicXML file itself and sends it to the API, which saves it in MongoDB as a song. An image or PDF goes to the API as a sheet. The API sends it to homr for the notes, then to Gemini for the chords, the title and the tempo, and sends the progress back to the browser through a subscription. Songs are kept in MongoDB for 30 days.
reading.legend_dashed: progress, sent back through a subscription
reading.legend_green: a MIDI or MusicXML file the browser has already read
reading.title: How a song gets in

sound.description: The browser turns the song’s notes into an outline with the tempo, the beats in a bar and where notes start. A text model on the API arranges the song from it once, choosing the sound, the drums, the look and the drum sections, and the song keeps that arrangement. Tone.js puts every note on its timeline after a two-second lead-in. The sound you picked plays through its tone, echo and reverb, and the drums go straight to the output.
sound.title: From the outline to the speakers
